newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Crude builds seen in APIs to mid-March.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Crude builds seen in APIs to mid-March.

text.p: This evening's oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected to show the fifth consecutive build in crude stocks, and the builds could continue into mid-March, industry sources said.
"We expect a seasonal creep up in crude stocks until mid-March, at least until refinery turnarounds are finished," said Theodore Eck, Amoco Corp's chief economist.
Traders expect crude stocks to grow between one and three million barrels for the week ended February 21.

Several refiners deferred maintenance in autumn to make distillate, making this winter's seasonal maintenance schedule busier than the last two years, with similar crude demand deterioration compared to prior years, dealers said.

The refinery utilization rate is seen up 0.5 percentage point to 88.8 percent but still below the last two years when it was 88.9 percent. The run rate had been 1.1 percentage point below a year ago for the week ended February 14.
"The market has acknowledged that crude stocks would be higher for the time being, and that's why we are off $6.00 (a barrel) from January," said Chevron Corp analyst Pat Hughes.

With the price drop in crude, Iraq is able to export more crude under the pricing formula of its oil-for-food agreement with the United Nations. The prospect of more Iraqi crude is, in fact, more bearish than rising crude stocks in the API data, traders said.

"That's more destabilizing than anything else out there right now," said one crude dealer of Iraq's ability to export Traders said crude stocks will decline when refineries emerge from maintenance to make gasoline for the summer driving season.
"I am watching to see if implied demand for gasoline stays firm. If it does, this could signal restocking on the secondary level," said Chevron's Hughes.

Indeed, gasoline stocks were seen flat to rising one million barrels, with growth restrained by demand. Demand was expected to remain near 7.4 million barrels a day after bottoming at 6.7 million for the week ended February 7.
Distillate stocks (comprised of heating oil and diesel) were expected to decline by one to two million barrels, a seasonal decline as refiners cut distillate production as winter draws to a close.
